intro.junior: Your body is made of about 37 trillion cells. Each one has tiny parts called organelles, and each organelle has a job, like rooms in a factory.

text.junior: A thin, flexible skin around the cell that controls what goes in and out.
The control centre. It holds DNA, the instructions for building and running the cell.
A dense spot inside the nucleus where ribosomes are made.
The cell's power stations. They use oxygen and glucose to release energy in cellular respiration.
Folded membranes around the nucleus. Rough ER, dotted with ribosomes, helps make proteins; smooth ER makes lipids.
A stack of flattened sacs that sorts, packages and sends proteins to where they are needed, like a post office.
Tiny machines that read instructions copied from DNA and build proteins.
Small sacs of enzymes that break down waste and worn-out cell parts.

intro.junior: Cells come in different shapes because they do different jobs. Compare these four.

text.junior: Long and branched, so it can carry electrical messages over long distances to many other cells.
A flexible, dimple-shaped disc packed with haemoglobin to carry oxygen. It has no nucleus, leaving more room for haemoglobin, and it can squeeze through the narrowest capillaries.
Long and striped, with many nuclei. It contains filaments that slide together so the cell can contract.
Lives inside hard bone and reaches out with many thin branches to its neighbours, helping keep the bone healthy.
